posts.author: vu2sga
posts.content_md:
Hello everybody,

I am relatively new to practical holography. I have been making reflection holograms for couple of months now with reasonably good results. I tried making transmission hologram for the first time today and I thought result was not bad for a first trial. Thought I would share the beginner's excitment with you all. 

Also I thought I could use some advise on photographing transmission holograms. My attempt to photograph this hologram using a digital camera has yielded a so-so result. Do have a look at [http://www.flickr.com/photos/21630907@N ... 002222117/](http://www.flickr.com/photos/21630907@N05/3067508979/in/set-72157609002222117/) . Any suggestions/comments?

Sanjay

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: That's a pretty good picture of a very good transmission hologram! Very little speckle in the pic, and I'm certain that if the reference beam was farther from the object, the exposure for the picture would be better. Excellent result for a first go at it!

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
Well done on your first transmission hologram. I remember the excitement when I made my first one!

It is interesting to find out the origin of the fringes on all the objects. I thought this might be due to two wavelengths, which would give you a kind of depth contour, but I think it is all the objects moving. But I am not sure. What you need to do is to make sure the objects are really settled and still before you shoot. The object just to the left of the coin seems to be paper, which is crumpled and moves irregularly during exposure.

posts.author: vu2sga
posts.content_md:
Hi,

The object to the left of the coin is actually a ceramic frog. So perhaps the fringes are being caused by two wavelengths in the beam. Thanks for pointing the possible causes.

Also thanks BobH for your suggestions regarding the photography.

Cheers!

Sanjay

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
That is interesting. I have not seen any of my 5mm diodes mode hop. Make sure to leave it on for about 15 minutes befor you shoot. I did see some holograms about ten years ago that had banding and the holographer was using a computer to turn on the diode as a shutter. This left the diode too instable to record a hologram. Your hologram really looks like the laser mode hopped during the exposure. This happens as the diodes warms up of if a blast of warm or cold air hits the diode.

Let me know if you see this again.
